summary: MissionForge is an interactive web game where players design, launch and manage a complete space mission, from objective to post-mission analysis. Players choose a scenario (Earth climate monitoring, a lunar water prospector, a Mars weather orbiter, or an asteroid flyby), then select a launch vehicle, orbit, spacecraft subsystems and science instruments. A live dashboard tracks mass, power, budget, data and communications, so every decision shows its consequences immediately. A launch check blocks unsafe designs with plain-language explanations of what broke, why, and how to fix it. The mission is then simulated with seeded random hazards such as solar flares and comms outages, scored, and followed by a root-cause report. Team mode supports up to four players in real time, each owning a role (Mission Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Officer, Comms and Ops) with competing goals, change requests and a unanimous ready-check before launch. Tutorials, tooltips, difficulty levels and a sandbox make it accessible to beginners. MissionForge makes the trade-offs of real mission design tangible, helping students learn how engineers balance competing demands as a team.
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

MissionForge turns space mission design into a playable experience. A player picks a scenario, then chooses a launch vehicle, orbit, spacecraft subsystems (structure, solar arrays, battery, communications, computer, attitude control, propulsion) and science instruments. A pure TypeScript engine recalculates mass, power (including eclipse battery depth of discharge), data generation versus downlink capacity, cost and mission lifetime on every change, and a live dashboard shows the result. A launch check blocks designs that break a constraint and explains what broke, why, and how to fix it. The mission is then simulated over time with seeded random events (solar flares, ground-station outages, sensor drift). Whether an event is mitigated depends on the design, for example a radiation-hardened computer survives a flare that resets a commercial one. A score and a root-cause report follow, with links to short concept explainers.

TEAM MODE

Up to four players join a room by code and each owns a role: Mission Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Officer, and Comms and Ops. Each role controls part of the design and has its own goal, and those goals conflict, so players negotiate through change requests, chat and a change log. Launch needs every player to press Ready, and any design change resets it. A server holds the shared state and runs the same engine as the client, so every player sees identical results.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Students rarely get to experiment with a whole mission. MissionForge lets them make decisions, see consequences immediately, fail safely, and learn why. There is no single perfect design, since a cheap CubeSat and an expensive flagship can both succeed, which reflects how real engineering works. Tutorials, tooltips, three difficulty levels and a sandbox make it usable by beginners and by more advanced learners, including in a classroom with shareable design links.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, Node.js, Express, Socket.IO, Vitest (55 automated tests), and SVG for the orbit and eclipse visualization. It is deployed as a single Node service. We used an AI coding assistant (Gemini in Google Antigravity) for implementation, working from a phased plan and requirements that we defined, and we reviewed and tested the results.

CREATIVITY

Role-based teamwork with deliberately conflicting goals, design-dependent hazards, a teaching-first validation system, an animated orbit and eclipse view tied to the simulation, and shareable design links.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Accessibility for non-experts, honest simplification of the physics so trade-offs stay clear, reproducibility through seeded randomness, fairness of scoring across different strategies, and keeping the engine separate from the interface so the same logic runs in solo and team play. Part specifications and mission scenarios are simplified and illustrative, inspired by missions such as Aqua, LRO and MAVEN, not real mission data.
